title: spike-recovery-efficiency-bench-notes-oct07-2027
body:
Purpose:
Quick working notes on the spike-recovery efficiency experiments we ran on 2027-10-03 -> 2027-10-06. Goal: quantify tradeoffs between aggressive autoscaling + prewarm vs conservative scaling + longer tail latency, and express cost as $/1k token-equivalents during and immediately after a spike. Draft for discussion — rough charts in text form, open Qs at the bottom.

Experiment summary:
- Workload: synthetic conversational workload modeled on product chat with heavy short-turn messages. 80% requests are 8–24 tokens, 20% are long (100–400 tokens).
- Spike shape: 0->peak 2.5k rps over 30s, sustained 90s, then exponential decay back to baseline over 6 minutes. We ran 6 repeats across 3 configs.
- Hardware: 8-GPU pool (A100-like), same model variant across runs (quantized 4-bit), identical KV cache settings unless noted.
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (ms), recovery-half-life (time to 50% drop from peak rps to baseline rps after scaling begins), cost-accumulator ($ spent during window), amortized $/1k-tokens for spike-window and recovery-window.

Configs tested (labels used below):
1) fast-prewarm: aggressive prewarm (20% idle reserved), scale-step 2x, immediate prewarm on scaling trigger
2) gradual-scale: conservative autoscale, step 1.2x, rely on on-demand warm-ups, no reserved prewarm
3) cache-boost: same as gradual-scale but with warm KV cache snapshots restored to new nodes (fast cache transfer)

High-level ascii summary (p95 latency in ms, per second timeline simplified):
Timescale: [0s..420s] (0..7min) spike begins at ~10s, peak at 40s, sustained until 130s, decays to baseline by ~430s
fast-prewarm p95 (ms):
baseline: 80
ramp-up (10-40s): 120 -> 240
peak (40-130s): 200
early-recovery (130-220s): 140 -> 100
late-recovery (220-430s): 90 -> 82

gradual-scale p95 (ms):
baseline: 78
ramp-up: 140 -> 380 (sharp spikes at new alloc events)
peak: 380 (many queued microbursts)
early-recovery: 220 -> 160
late-recovery: 110 -> 85

cache-boost p95 (ms):
baseline: 82
ramp-up: 110 -> 190
peak: 160
early-recovery: 120 -> 92
late-recovery: 86 -> 80

Observed recovery-half-life (seconds from end-of-sustain to 50% rps drop):
- fast-prewarm: 58s
- gradual-scale: 185s
- cache-boost: 72s

Cost ($) summary for window (0s..600s around experiment) expressed as platform compute spend (not including network/storage):
- fast-prewarm: $24.8 total, amortized $3.9 per 1k-tokens during spike+recovery window
- gradual-scale: $15.6 total, amortized $6.4 per 1k-tokens (higher token-cost because long tail of latency reduced throughput and more token-timeouts retried)
- cache-boost: $19.2 total, amortized $4.6 per 1k-tokens

Interpretation notes (rough):
- aggressive prewarm (fast-prewarm) increases baseline spend but reduces tail latencies and recovery time significantly; cost per token during spike+recovery is lowest because throughput is maintained and retries are minimal.
- gradual-scale looks cheaper in steady-state but results in a long drag on throughput and heavy p99/p95 inflation during ramp; the longer tail causes more retries and perceived client failures which increases effective token-cost.
- cache-boost captures much of the latency benefit of prewarm with less baseline spend — restoring KV cache quickly reduces cold-kv penalty which helps p95/p99 during ramp and peak.

Text table: (rough columns: config | baseline-cost($/min) | peak-delay-ms | recover-half-life-s | $/1k-token-spike)
fast-prewarm | 0.41 | 200 | 58 | 3.9
gradual-scale | 0.26 | 380 | 185 | 6.4
cache-boost | 0.32 | 160 | 72 | 4.6

Representative percentile breakdown (fast-prewarm run #3):
- p50: 58ms
- p90: 112ms
- p95: 200ms
- p99: 420ms (these p99s are dominated by a tiny fraction of requests during allocation events)

Qualitative observations and mitigations:
- Prewarm cost is mostly idle GPU minutes; for predictable spikes (scheduled marketing events) prewarm is clearly worth it. Action: add simple schedule API for reserving N slots for known windows. (JIRA:INF-PR-207)
- KV cache transfer approach matters — cold-kv penalty (~150ms median delta) stacks with allocation overhead. Invest in snapshot-and-restore + delta sync to new nodes. (See linked PR)
- Autoscale step granularity: 1.2x steps can underprovision and cause long tails; but large steps cause overprovisioning waste. Suggest exploring adaptive step sizes driven by queue-length derivative (not just rate).
- Graceful-degradation policy: for long-recovery runs we observed clients hitting retry behavior that amplified load briefly. Implement client-aware backoff guidance and server-side request-shedding thresholds for non-priority routes.

Actionable recommendations (priority):
1) short-term (S1, 2–4 weeks): expose prewarm scheduling for customer API + telemetry; add experiment flag to enable cache-boost snapshot restore in new pools.
2) medium-term (M1, 1–3 months): implement queue-derivative autoscale policy and run canary vs current step-scaler; add autoscale simulations in platform CI.
3) long-term (M2, 3–6 months): evaluate fine-grained slot packing to reduce idle-reserve cost and enable ephemeral prewarm (reserve fractional GPUs via colocated micro-shards).

Open questions and data needs:
- Need to repeat with multi-tenant interference enabled (we ran single-tenant runs). How does cache-restore behave when KV namespace collides?
- How sensitive are results to model size and quantization? We used one quant profile; run same set for a medium and a large model.
- Gather real traffic replay from last marketing spike (INF-analytics dump) and run to validate synthetic workload assumptions.

Notes to reviewers: rough numbers above — some runs had flaky telemetry capture for p99 (see run #2 in linked artifacts). I'm splitting the raw CSVs into confluence tables next. If you want the ascii-run charts with more granularity (per-second p95), tell me which run to export.

Next steps: assign S1 tasks to Priya for prewarm API proto, Ethan to wire cache snapshot toggle into staging, Diego to open autoscale-sim ticket with initial queue-derivative heuristics.

Small informal log (raw):
- 2027-10-03 09:12 — started run, noticed two allocation failures; retried cluster scale commands
- 2027-10-04 15:05 — cache-boost snapshots applied, p95 improved ~30% during ramp
- 2027-10-06 11:47 — re-run with 20% longer sustain, observed gradual-scale p99 blowout

End of draft.
